title: Behaviour as a Value: What a Lambda Captures, and For How Long

questions.question: Two lambdas are made while limit is 1.0. Then limit becomes 100.0. Asked whether 50 exceeds the limit, what does each say?
options: Both say true: a capture is taken when the lambda is created
[limit] says true, answering against its own copy of 1.0; [&limit] says false, reading 100.0 at the call
Both say false: the limit is 100 by the time either is called
[limit] fails to compile, because limit is not const
questions.explanation: A by value capture is a decision taken once. A by reference capture is a question asked every call. Neither is wrong; they are different things, and one character separates them.

questions.question: Does returning a lambda that captured a local by reference produce a compiler diagnostic?
options: Only clang warns, through -Wreturn-stack-address
Yes, both refuse it, as they do for returning a reference to a local
No: measured with -Wall -Wextra -Werror, gcc and clang both accepted it
Yes, it is a hard error in C++17
questions.explanation: Returning a reference to a local directly is refused by both, and lesson 01-11 keeps that in checks/. Hide the same reference inside a capture list and the diagnostic disappears. The address sanitizer does find it at runtime, which is why the lane exists.

questions.question: What is sizeof a lambda that captures nothing, and why?
options: 1 byte: it is a class with no members, and an empty class still needs a distinct address
8 bytes: it holds a pointer to its own code
32 bytes, the same as a std::function
0 bytes: there is nothing to store
questions.explanation: A lambda is a class the compiler writes, with one member per capture. Measured: nothing is 1 byte, one double is 8, one reference is 8, and a whole captured std::vector is 24, which is sizeof(std::vector<double>).

questions.question: Are two character for character identical lambda expressions the same type?
options: Only within the same function
Yes, since they have the same signature
Yes, if they capture the same things
No: the compiler writes a new class for every lambda expression in the program
questions.explanation: Which is why you store one with auto: the type has no name you could write down. It is also why putting one into a std::function is a conversion rather than a copy.

questions.question: A std::function holding a lambda that captures 17 bytes allocated once, while one capturing 8 bytes allocated none. What allocated, and when?
options: std::function, on every call
The lambda, when it was created
The lambda, on every call
std::function, when it was assigned, because what it holds did not fit in its internal buffer
questions.explanation: The lambda never allocates: 64 bytes of captures is a 64 byte object on the stack, and calling it directly cost 0. The allocation comes from type erasure needing somewhere to keep an object whose size is not known until runtime, and it happens at assignment, so build the callback outside the loop.

questions.question: Capturing a std::vector by value in a lambda that is then stored in a std::function cost 3 allocations. Why three?
options: std::function always allocates three times
One per element, for the first three elements
The vector's buffer was copied into the lambda, and then the lambda was too big to live inside the std::function
The vector was copied three times, once per capture
questions.explanation: Two costs for one capture list. Against 0 allocations for the callable that captured a single double. Capture a pointer to the data rather than the data, after answering the lifetime question that raises.
